tierWindow.goal: Write with argument, structure and sources: shape an argumentative essay, integrate academic sources so they support your own argument, and give your writing a critical edge.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Application and analysis (structure, integrate, construct and develop), building on the recognition and recall the introductory tier taught.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Multi-part tasks held together at once: an argument sustained across an essay's paragraphs, several sources woven into a single paragraph, criticality carried through word choice.
tierWindow.autonomy: Moderate scaffolding; worked examples model each move, but the learner is expected to make the move rather than only recognise it.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner can already treat writing as a staged process and get a readable first draft down, which is the introductory tier. They have not yet learned to shape an argument across a whole essay, to weave sources into their own argument, or to give writing a critical edge; teach these as the step up from a competent draft, not from scratch.

subThemes.label: Writing agility: writing successfully across the genres different assessments ask for
The argumentative essay: a continuous response shaped as an argument to a question
How the argument emerges from structure: introduction, body and conclusion, and the topic sentence within each paragraph
Using sources actively to support your argument rather than reporting what they say
The voices technique: weaving several sources into a paragraph with the author's voice leading
Developing a critical edge: being critical from the first reading and linking, comparing and evaluating sources
Flagging criticality in writing: the language of criticality as beacons that signal a critical move to the reader

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, the argumentative essay: how structure carries an argument from introduction to conclusion. Second, integrating academic sources: using the voices technique so sources support your argument. Third, developing a critical edge: engaging actively with what you read and signalling your criticality. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about writing with argument, structure and sources. You can already treat writing as a process and get a draft down. The next step is shaping that draft into an argument. By the end you will be able to structure an argumentative essay, integrate academic sources so they support your argument, and give your writing a critical edge.

These are not abstract study skills. Most of your marks come from written argument, in every subject. Shaping a case, using sources well, and showing your criticality are what lift a competent draft into strong academic work.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: structure an argumentative essay, integrate sources to support the argument, give writing a critical edge.

practiceConnection.academic: Written argument is how most of your learning is judged. Every essay that asks you to assess, discuss or evaluate wants a position held together across paragraphs and supported by sources you have weighed. Build these habits now and they carry into every module of your degree, and into the reasoned, well-evidenced writing that professional work later asks of you.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced academic writing course takes these skills into writing within your own discipline, where the conventions of your subject shape how you argue. Going wider: the same habits underpin Criticality, Referencing and Researching, where you put argument, sources and a critical edge to work on real tasks. If any part still feels new, the introductory course revisits the writing process and the basics.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Your writing can now carry an argument. You can structure an argumentative essay so its introduction, body and conclusion hold one case, with each paragraph making a single point that moves the argument forward. You can integrate sources using the voices technique, keeping your own voice in charge so sources support your argument rather than replace it. And you can give your writing a critical edge, using sources actively and signalling your judgements with the language of criticality. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, writing with argument is something you do in every module. Each essay you shape around one case, each paragraph where your own voice leads the sources, each judgement you signal rather than leave implied, is this course at work. It is also what professional life rewards: clear, reasoned, well-evidenced writing that takes a position and defends it travels well beyond your degree.
